claims.text: The initial material is as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has reported tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has inadequate inherent resistance to oxygen attack.
Electrospark deposition can produce a coating from an HfNbTaTiZr electrode material.
An HfNbTaTiZr electrospark coating can be deposited as a thin, adherent layer on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed coating may instead use a slightly modified HfNbTaTiZr variant optimized for oxide-scale formation.
The deposited coating will be continuous and adherent.
The coating will form a dense, slow-growing protective oxide layer.
The protective oxide layer will impede oxygen diffusion into the substrate.
Electrospark deposition creates a microstructure conducive to rapid formation of the protective oxide scale.
The coating will significantly reduce oxidation of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr in air at 800–1000 °C for exposures up to 5 hours.
Reduced oxidation will be manifested by lower weight gain, a thinner oxide layer, and minimal surface degradation relative to untreated material.
The coating will preserve useful room-temperature and high-temperature tensile properties.
Uncoated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr undergoes significant oxidation or pesting and associated mechanical-property degradation in high-temperature air.
The proposed benefit is limited to air exposures at 800–1000 °C for no more than 5 hours.
The cited study fabricated an HfNbTaTiZr electrospark-deposition coating on stainless steel and tested it electrochemically in 3.5% NaCl solution.
The supporting evidence includes results from a non-equiatomic alloy system.
Saline electrochemical corrosion results do not directly establish high-temperature oxidation protection, coating adhesion, or compatibility under thermal cycling for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant oxidation reduction or any loss of mechanical properties relative to the uncoated control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions imply high-temperature exposure under strain rates similar to prior mechanical tests, whereas the falsification experiment describes an apparently unloaded oxidation exposure followed by separate tensile testing. The loading boundary during oxidation is therefore inconsistent or undefined.
